At the heart of every use of "strip" is one powerful idea: removal that leaves something bare, exposed, or empty. When you strip something, you are not just taking a little away — you are removing a layer, a covering, a possession, or a quality, often completely. Think of it as peeling away until what remains is raw and uncovered.

1. To Remove Clothing

The most familiar use of "strip" is to take clothes off — either your own or someone else's.

  • She stripped off her wet jacket the moment she got home.
  • The doctor asked him to strip to the waist so she could examine his back.
  • He stripped and jumped into the river.

Notice that "strip" suggests removing clothes quickly or completely, not just loosening a button. It carries a sense of thorough removal. The phrase "strip down" is very common here and means to undress to minimal or no clothing: "They stripped down before getting into the pool."

A "stripper" is a person who removes their clothes as a performance — this comes directly from this meaning.

2. To Remove a Surface Layer or Covering from Something

You can strip a surface — meaning you remove whatever is coating it to expose what lies underneath.

  • We stripped the old paint from the walls before repainting.
  • He spent the afternoon stripping wallpaper from the bedroom.
  • The deer had stripped the bark off several trees.
  • Strip the leaves from the stems before putting the flowers in a vase.

The key here is that something on top of or around another thing is being removed. The wall, tree, or stem still exists — you are just removing what was covering it.

3. To Remove Everything from a Place or Object

"Strip" can also mean to take everything out of or off something, leaving it completely bare or empty — like a skeleton picked clean.

  • Thieves broke in and stripped the apartment of every valuable item.
  • The mechanics stripped the old car down to its bare frame.
  • Locusts stripped the fields, leaving nothing behind.

This meaning often appears with the phrase "strip something of something" — meaning to remove all contents or all value from it. It has a sense of thoroughness bordering on destruction.

4. To Take Away a Title, Right, Rank, or Privilege

Here, "strip" is used figuratively for taking something abstract away from someone — something they have earned, hold, or own by status.

  • The court stripped him of his citizenship.
  • She was stripped of her gold medal after failing the drugs test.
  • The scandal led to the general being stripped of his rank.
  • The new law stripped citizens of several key protections.

The structure is almost always: strip someone of something. The thing being taken away is not physical — it is a title, a status, a right, or a privilege. Notice how this carries a harsh tone: stripping something from someone implies that the removal is forceful, often punitive, and leaves them diminished or exposed — just like the other meanings of the word.

5. To Damage the Threads of a Screw or Gear (Mechanical)

In mechanics and engineering, you can "strip" a screw, bolt, or gear. This means the grooves (called threads) on the screw or the teeth on the gear get worn down or broken — usually from too much force or using the wrong tool.

  • Be careful not to overtighten it or you'll strip the screw.
  • He used too much force and stripped the bolt.
  • The gearbox failed because a gear had been stripped.

A stripped screw is essentially ruined — it can no longer be tightened or loosened properly because the grooves that a screwdriver grips are gone. The word fits perfectly: the screw has been "stripped" of the very feature that made it functional.

6. To Remove Insulation from a Wire (Electrical)

This is a specific but very common technical use. An electrical wire is usually coated in a protective layer of rubber or plastic. Before you can connect a wire to anything, you must remove that coating at the end to expose the metal conductor inside.

  • Use wire strippers to strip the ends of the cable.
  • He stripped about two centimetres of insulation from each wire.

This is simply a specialized version of meaning #2 — removing a coating to expose what's underneath — but it appears so frequently in everyday contexts (home repairs, electronics, etc.) that it is worth knowing separately.

7. To Separate Something from Something Else

More broadly, "strip" can mean to separate a substance or element from whatever it is attached to or mixed with — common in cooking, farming, and industry.

  • Strip the corn kernels off the cob.
  • The machine strips seeds from the raw cotton.
  • Strip the meat from the bones.

Again, the idea is the same: you are removing one thing from another, leaving them separated.

"Strip away" — to remove something in order to reveal what is truly underneath. This is often used figuratively to cut through complexity or pretense:

  • If you strip away all the complicated language, the argument is actually very simple.
  • Grief can strip away everything you thought was important.

"Strip down" — to reduce something to only its most basic and essential form:

  • Let's strip down this plan to what really matters.
  • The engineers stripped down the engine to diagnose the problem.

"Strip" almost always implies that what remains after the action is bare, raw, and exposed. Whether it's a person without clothes, a wall without paint, a soldier without rank, or a field without crops — something has been removed and what is left behind is unprotected and uncovered. This gives the word a slight edge: it is more forceful and more complete than softer words like remove or take off. When something is stripped, it is not gently unwrapped — it is fully and thoroughly cleared.
